module_title: Soil Fertility and Crop Nutrient Requirements

lessons.title: Essential Plant Nutrients and Their Roles
lessons.body:
Plants need 17 essential nutrients to grow and produce well. Three of theseâcarbon, hydrogen, and oxygenâcome from air and water. The other 14 come from the soil. If any one is missing, even if all others are present, plant growth will be limited. That is why we blend fertilizers: to supply the nutrients that are lacking in the soil.

The main nutrients are divided into macronutrients (needed in large amounts) and micronutrients (needed in tiny amounts). The primary macronutrients are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). Nitrogen drives leaf and stem growth and gives plants their dark green color. Phosphorus is critical for root development, flowering, and seed formation. Potassium strengthens stems, improves drought tolerance, and helps fight disease. Secondary macronutrientsâcalcium, magnesium, and sulfurâare needed in smaller amounts but are still vital. Calcium builds strong cell walls, magnesium is at the center of chlorophyll, and sulfur helps form proteins.

Micronutrients include iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine, and nickel. Although plants need them in very small quantities, a shortage can cause serious problems. For example, zinc deficiency in maize causes white bands on leaves and stunted growth. Boron deficiency in tomatoes leads to hollow stems and cracked fruit. In many African soils, zinc and boron are often deficient, especially in sandy or heavily weathered soils.

Each nutrient has a specific role, and they work together. For instance, too much nitrogen can cause plants to grow leaves at the expense of roots or fruits. Too little phosphorus can delay maturity. A balanced blend considers the soilâs supply and the cropâs demand. In practice, you will use soil tests and crop knowledge to decide which nutrients to include and in what ratios. Remember: a fertilizer blend is only as good as its weakest component. If one nutrient is missing, the others cannot do their job fully.

lessons.title: Soil Testing and Interpretation
lessons.body:
Soil testing is the foundation of good fertilizer blending. Without it, you are guessing. A soil test tells you the pH, organic matter, and available levels of key nutrients like phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, and micronutrients. In Africa, many extension services and private labs offer soil testing. The cost is usually between $20 and $50 per sample, which is small compared to the cost of wasted fertilizer.

To take a good sample, use a clean auger or spade. Collect 15 to 20 sub-samples from different spots in a field, going to a depth of 15â20 cm for annual crops. Mix them in a clean bucket, then take about 500 g of the mixed soil and send it to a lab. Avoid sampling near fences, animal pens, or where fertilizer was heaped. Sample at the same time each year, preferably before planting.

The lab report will give you numbers, often in parts per million (ppm) or kg/ha. You need to interpret these against critical levels. For example, for maize in many African soils, the critical level for phosphorus (Olsen P) is about 10â15 ppm. If your soil tests below that, you need to add phosphorus. Potassium critical levels are often around 100â150 ppm. The report will also give a pH reading. Most crops grow best between pH 5.8 and 6.8. If pH is below 5.5, you may need lime; if above 7.5, you may need gypsum or elemental sulfur.

Interpretation also depends on soil texture. Sandy soils leach nutrients quickly and hold few nutrients, so they need more frequent, smaller applications. Clay soils hold nutrients better but may fix phosphorus. Organic matter improves nutrient holding. Use the soil test to calculate how much nutrient to add: if the soil supplies 10 kg/ha of P and your crop needs 30 kg/ha, you need to add 20 kg/ha of P. Always adjust for the fertilizerâs analysis (e.g., DAP is 18% N and 46% P2O5).

lessons.title: Crop-Specific Nutrient Uptake Patterns
lessons.body:
Different crops remove different amounts of nutrients from the soil, and they take them up at different times. Knowing these patterns helps you design blends that match the cropâs needs. For example, maize is a heavy feeder. A crop yielding 5 tonnes per hectare removes about 120 kg N, 50 kg P2O5, and 100 kg K2O. It takes up most nitrogen during the rapid vegetative growth stage (V6 to tasseling). Phosphorus is critical early for root development, while potassium is needed throughout but especially during grain filling.

Legumes like beans, groundnuts, and soybeans fix their own nitrogen through rhizobia bacteria, so they need little or no nitrogen fertilizer. However, they need good phosphorus and potassium, plus sulfur and micronutrients like molybdenum and boron. For example, a 2-tonne groundnut crop removes about 40 kg N, 20 kg P2O5, and 40 kg K2O, but the nitrogen is mostly replaced by fixation. Applying nitrogen to legumes is wasteful and can reduce nodulation.

Root and tuber crops like cassava, sweet potato, and yam have high potassium demands. Cassava yielding 20 tonnes per hectare removes about 100 kg N, 40 kg P2O5, and 150 kg K2O. Potassium is crucial for starch formation and tuber bulking. They also need adequate phosphorus for root initiation. Vegetables like tomatoes and peppers are heavy feeders of all three macronutrients, plus calcium to prevent blossom-end rot. A tomato crop yielding 40 tonnes per hectare may remove 150 kg N, 60 kg P2O5, and 200 kg K2O.

Timing matters as much as amount. Split applications of nitrogen are better than one large dose, especially in sandy soils. For maize, apply half at planting and half at knee-high. For cassava, apply all phosphorus and potassium at planting and split nitrogen. Always consider the cropâs growth cycle: annual crops need nutrients within a few months, while perennials like banana or oil palm need regular applications. By matching nutrient supply to uptake patterns, you increase efficiency and reduce losses.

lessons.title: Determining Nutrient Ratios for Blends
lessons.body:
A fertilizer blend is a mixture of different nutrient sources to achieve a desired ratio of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K), plus possibly secondary and micronutrients. The ratio is expressed as N-P2O5-K2O, such as 15-15-15 or 20-10-10. To determine the right ratio, you need three things: the soil test results, the cropâs nutrient requirements, and the target yield.

Start by calculating the amount of each nutrient the crop needs for your yield goal. For example, if you want 4 tonnes of maize per hectare, you need about 100 kg N, 40 kg P2O5, and 80 kg K2O. Next, subtract the nutrients the soil already supplies (from the soil test). If the soil test shows 10 kg/ha of available P2O5 and 60 kg/ha of K2O, then you need to add 30 kg P2O5 and 20 kg K2O. For nitrogen, soil supply is harder to measure, so assume you need the full 100 kg N.

Now you have a required ratio: 100 N : 30 P2O5 : 20 K2O. Simplify by dividing by the smallest number (20): 5 : 1.5 : 1. This is close to a 5:1.5:1 ratio. Common blend ratios in Africa include 23-21-0+4S for maize in some areas, or 15-15-15 for general use. But a custom blend may be better. For example, a 20-10-10 blend would supply 100 kg N, 50 kg P2O5, and 50 kg K2O per 500 kg of product. That might be too much P and K if your soil is already high.

To make the blend, you mix granular fertilizers like urea (46-0-0), DAP (18-46-0), muriate of potash (0-0-60), and filler. You must ensure the granules are compatible and not reactive. For small-scale farmers, it may be easier to buy pre-blended fertilizers or use straight fertilizers separately. But understanding ratios helps you choose the right product. Always check the label: a 15-15-15 blend has 15% N, 15% P2O5, and 15% K2O. If you need more nitrogen, you can supplement with urea.

lessons.title: Yield Goals and Nutrient Budgeting
lessons.body:
A yield goal is the amount of harvest you realistically expect from a field. It should be based on past yields, soil potential, water availability, and management level. Setting a yield goal helps you calculate how much fertilizer to apply. If you aim too high, you waste money; too low, you lose potential income. In Africa, many smallholders achieve 1â2 tonnes of maize per hectare, but with good management, 4â6 tonnes is possible.

Nutrient budgeting is the process of balancing nutrient inputs (fertilizer, manure, compost, crop residues) with nutrient outputs (harvest removal, leaching, erosion). The goal is to avoid depleting soil nutrients. For each field, estimate the nutrients removed by the crop. For example, a 3-tonne maize crop removes about 75 kg N, 30 kg P2O5, and 60 kg K2O. If you apply 100 kg of 15-15-15, you add 15 kg N, 15 kg P2O5, and 15 kg K2Oâfar less than removed. So you need additional nitrogen, likely as urea.

To budget, start with the yield goal. Use tables or software (like the Africa Soil Information Service or local extension charts) to find nutrient removal per tonne of yield. Then subtract nutrients supplied by soil (from soil test) and organic amendments. The difference is what you need from fertilizer. For example, if you apply 5 tonnes of cattle manure per hectare, it might supply 25 kg N, 10 kg P2O5, and 30 kg K2O, but release is slow. Account for that.

Also consider residual effects: phosphorus and potassium can build up in soil, so you may not need to apply them every year. Nitrogen is mobile and must be applied each season. A nutrient budget helps you avoid over- or under-fertilizing. Keep records of yields and fertilizer applied. After a few seasons, you can adjust your goals and blends. This is the path to sustainable intensification.

lessons.title: Environmental Factors Affecting Nutrient Availability
lessons.body:
Even if a nutrient is present in the soil, it may not be available to plants. Several environmental factors control availability. The most important are soil pH, organic matter, moisture, temperature, and aeration. Understanding these helps you manage fertilizers better.

Soil pH affects nutrient solubility. At pH below 5.5, phosphorus binds with iron and aluminum, becoming unavailable. At pH above 7.5, phosphorus binds with calcium. Micronutrients like zinc, iron, and manganese are less available at high pH, while molybdenum is less available at low pH. Most nutrients are most available between pH 6.0 and 7.0. In Africa, many soils are acidic (pH 4.5â5.5), so liming is often necessary to raise pH and unlock phosphorus.

Organic matter is a reservoir of nutrients and improves soil structure. It holds water and nutrients, and its decomposition releases nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, and micronutrients slowly. Sandy soils with less than 1% organic matter have low nutrient holding capacity. Adding manure or compost increases organic matter and improves availability.

Soil moisture is critical. Nutrients move to roots by diffusion and mass flow, which require water. In drought, nutrients cannot reach roots, and fertilizer may not dissolve. Conversely, waterlogged soils become anaerobic, causing nitrogen loss through denitrification and making iron and manganese toxic. Temperature affects microbial activity: in cold soils, organic matter decomposition is slow, so less nitrogen is released. In hot, dry soils, volatilization of ammonia from urea can be high.

Aeration affects root respiration and microbial processes. Compacted soils have poor aeration, limiting root growth and nutrient uptake. Erosion removes topsoil rich in nutrients. To manage these factors, use conservation tillage, add organic matter, apply lime based on soil test, and irrigate when possible. Also, place fertilizer near the roots (banding) rather than broadcasting, especially for phosphorus. By understanding environmental factors, you can choose the right fertilizer and timing to maximize availability.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a primary macronutrient?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen is one of the three primary macronutrients (N, P, K) needed in large amounts.

quiz.q: What is the main role of phosphorus in plants?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus is critical for root development, flowering, and seed formation.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient deficiency causes white bands on maize leaves?
quiz.explanation: Zinc deficiency in maize typically shows as white bands on leaves and stunted growth.

quiz.q: How many essential nutrients do plants need from the soil?
quiz.explanation: Of the 17 essential nutrients, 14 are taken up from the soil; the other three come from air and water.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost range for a soil test in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Soil testing in Africa usually costs between $20 and $50 per sample, a small investment compared to fertilizer waste.

quiz.q: What is the recommended soil sampling depth for annual crops?
quiz.explanation: For annual crops, soil samples should be taken from a depth of 15â20 cm where most roots and nutrients are found.

quiz.q: What does a soil pH of 5.0 indicate?
quiz.explanation: A pH below 7 is acidic; pH 5.0 is strongly acidic and may require liming.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most likely to be deficient in sandy soils?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils have low nutrient holding capacity and potassium is easily leached, making it often deficient.

quiz.q: How much nitrogen does a 5-tonne maize crop remove per hectare?
quiz.explanation: A 5-tonne maize crop removes about 120 kg N per hectare, along with other nutrients.

quiz.q: Why do legumes like beans need little or no nitrogen fertilizer?
options: B) They fix nitrogen from the air
C) They get nitrogen from soil
quiz.explanation: Legumes form symbiotic relationships with rhizobia bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen.

quiz.q: Which crop has the highest potassium demand?
quiz.explanation: Cassava, a root crop, has high potassium demand for starch formation and tuber bulking.

quiz.q: When is the best time to apply nitrogen to maize for maximum efficiency?
options: B) Split between planting and knee-high
quiz.explanation: Splitting nitrogen application reduces losses and matches uptake during rapid growth stages.

quiz.q: What does a fertilizer ratio of 15-15-15 mean?
quiz.explanation: The numbers represent the percentage of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P2O5), and potassium (K2O) by weight.

quiz.q: If a soil test shows 10 kg/ha of available P2O5 and the crop needs 40 kg/ha, how much P2O5 must be added?
quiz.explanation: Subtract soil supply from crop need: 40 â 10 = 30 kg/ha of P2O5 to add.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is commonly used as a nitrogen source in blends?
quiz.explanation: Urea (46-0-0) is a high-analysis nitrogen fertilizer often used in blends.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a filler in a fertilizer blend?
quiz.explanation: Fillers are inert materials used to adjust the final nutrient concentration to the desired ratio.

quiz.q: What is a realistic yield goal for smallholder maize in Africa with good management?
quiz.explanation: With good management, smallholders can achieve 4â6 tonnes of maize per hectare, though many currently get 1â2 tonnes.

quiz.q: What is nutrient budgeting?
options: B) Balancing nutrient inputs and outputs
quiz.explanation: Nutrient budgeting balances nutrients added (fertilizer, manure) against those removed by crops and lost.

quiz.q: How much nitrogen does 100 kg of 15-15-15 fertilizer supply?
quiz.explanation: 15% of 100 kg is 15 kg of nitrogen.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most mobile and must be applied each season?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen is mobile in soil, easily leached or volatilized, so it requires regular application.

quiz.q: At what soil pH range are most nutrients most available?
quiz.explanation: Most nutrients are most available to plants when soil pH is between 6.0 and 7.0.

quiz.q: What happens to phosphorus availability in very acidic soils (pH < 5.5)?
options: B) Decreases due to binding with iron and aluminum
quiz.explanation: In acidic soils, phosphorus binds with iron and aluminum, forming insoluble compounds unavailable to plants.

quiz.q: Which practice can help reduce nitrogen loss through volatilization?
options: A) Broadcasting urea on dry soil
C) Applying urea before heavy rain
quiz.explanation: Incorporating urea into the soil reduces ammonia volatilization loss.

quiz.q: What is the effect of waterlogging on nutrient availability?
options: B) Causes denitrification and loss of nitrogen
quiz.explanation: Waterlogged soils become anaerobic, leading to denitrification and nitrogen loss.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient becomes less available at high soil pH?
quiz.explanation: Zinc, iron, and manganese are less available at high pH, while molybdenum is less available at low pH.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of adding organic matter to soil?
quiz.explanation: Organic matter improves soil structure and increases the soil's ability to hold water and nutrients.

quiz.q: Why is banding phosphorus fertilizer better than broadcasting?
options: B) It places nutrients near roots
quiz.explanation: Banding places phosphorus close to roots, improving uptake because phosphorus is immobile in soil.

quiz.q: What does a soil test report typically include?
options: B) pH, organic matter, and nutrient levels
quiz.explanation: A soil test report provides pH, organic matter, and available nutrient levels like P, K, Ca, Mg.

quiz.q: Which crop is a heavy feeder of all three macronutrients?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes are heavy feeders of N, P, and K, and also need calcium to prevent blossom-end rot.

quiz.q: What is the critical level of Olsen P for maize in many African soils?
quiz.explanation: Below 10â15 ppm Olsen P, maize is likely to respond to phosphorus fertilizer.
